summary: Describes F-RTO, a sender-only algorithm for detecting spurious retransmission timeouts in TCP and SCTP. A spurious timeout causes unnecessary resending of data, which hurts performance. F-RTO needs no TCP options. The document is experimental.

eli5.summary: Sometimes you think a letter is lost and send another, but the first one was just slow. This memo helps computers notice that mistake so they do not waste time sending things twice.

subtitle: A sender-only trick for noticing that a TCP timeout was a false alarm, so the sender does not resend a whole window of data.

tldr.problem: A TCP retransmission timer can expire even though nothing was lost, for example after a sudden delay spike. The sender then unnecessarily retransmits the last window of data and floods the network when the late ACKs arrive.
tldr.mechanism: After retransmitting the first unacknowledged segment, the F-RTO sender sends new data and watches the next two acknowledgments. If both advance the window by acknowledging data that was not retransmitted, it declares the timeout spurious.
tldr.outcome: F-RTO avoids needless retransmissions after a spurious timeout and falls back to conventional RTO recovery otherwise. It is Experimental and is updated by RFC 5682.

today: RFC 4138 is Experimental and is updated by RFC 5682, so read that RFC for the current version of the algorithm. It has not been obsoleted according to the metadata.

sections.title: Spurious Timeouts and Why They Hurt
sections.content:
A TCP sender has two ways to trigger a retransmission: a number of duplicate ACKs, or the retransmission timeout (RTO) expiring. After an RTO, the sender sets its congestion window to one segment and retransmits unacknowledged segments using slow start.

A timeout is spurious if the sender would have avoided it by waiting longer for an acknowledgment. The RFC lists causes such as delay spikes during a mobile hand-off, a sudden rise in round-trip time when competing traffic arrives on a low-bandwidth link, and a persistently reliable link layer that loses a frame and its retransmissions. When this happens, the late ACKs of the original segments usually trigger unnecessary retransmission of a whole window. A conventional sender also grows its window on each late ACK in slow start, which injects many segments within one round-trip time and violates the packet conservation principle.
sections.eli5: Imagine you ask a friend a question, count to three, and ask again because they were quiet, but they were only thinking. Now they answer twice and you have to sort out the mess.

sections.title: The Basic F-RTO Algorithm
sections.content:
F-RTO changes sender behavior only after a retransmission timeout. A sender MAY implement it, but if it does, it MUST follow these steps. It SHOULD NOT enter F-RTO when earlier fast recovery is underway, if it uses a loss recovery algorithm other than Reno or NewReno.

Step 1: on RTO, retransmit the first unacknowledged segment, set SpuriousRecovery to FALSE, and store the highest sequence number sent so far in recover.

Step 2: on the first ACK after the retransmission, if it is a duplicate ACK, acknowledges recover, or does not acknowledge all the data retransmitted in step 1, revert to conventional RTO recovery. Otherwise, if it advances the window and is below recover, send up to two new, previously unsent segments and go to step 3. If there is no new data or the advertised window forbids sending, skip step 3 and continue with conventional slow start retransmissions.

Step 3: on the second ACK, if it is a duplicate, set the congestion window to no more than 3 * MSS and keep retransmitting in slow start. If it advances the window, acknowledging data that was not retransmitted, declare the timeout spurious, set SpuriousRecovery to SPUR_TO and set recover to SND.UNA.
sections.eli5: After the timer goes off, the sender resends one packet and then tries something new. If the replies show the old packets were just slow, it says it was a false alarm. If the replies look odd, it goes back to the usual careful way.

sections.title: Why the Algorithm Is Cautious
sections.content:
The RFC explains each guard. If the first ACK covers recover, there is not enough evidence that a non-retransmitted segment arrived. The RFC says this is a common case when a fast retransmission is lost and then retransmitted after an RTO. Requiring the first ACK to cover everything retransmitted in step 1 stops a malicious receiver acknowledging partial segments from making the sender declare a timeout spurious when data was lost.

Two new segments are allowed in step 2 because a conventional sender would also send two on the first new ACK after an RTO retransmission. Setting recover to SND.UNA after a spurious timeout allows fast retransmit if three duplicate ACKs arrive.

A side effect is that the sender can take round-trip time samples on the delayed segments, so the RTO is likely to be more accurate and larger after a spurious timeout. F-RTO may fail to detect a spurious timeout when packet reordering or duplication affects the triggering segment, or when the timeout happens during fast recovery. In those cases it falls back to slow start retransmissions and performs like the regular recovery.
sections.eli5: The sender only calls it a false alarm when the evidence is clear. When it is unsure, it plays safe, because guessing wrong could flood the network.

sections.title: The SACK-Enhanced Version
sections.content:
If the TCP Selective Acknowledgment option is enabled on a connection, a sender MAY implement the SACK-enhanced variant. It detects spurious timeouts in most cases where reordering or duplication produce duplicate ACKs, because SACK blocks can show that new data, which was not transmitted after the RTO retransmission, has arrived. It SHOULD NOT be applied if the sender is already in SACK loss recovery when the timeout occurs.

It has the same three-step shape. On timeout it retransmits the first unacknowledged segment and resets the SACK scoreboard. In step 2 it waits for the cumulative ACK of the retransmitted data, adjusting the scoreboard on duplicate ACKs, and then sends up to two new segments if the ACK is below recover. In step 3 it declares the timeout spurious if the ACK does not acknowledge anything above recover but does acknowledge data not acknowledged earlier, since that segment was sent before the timeout. Otherwise it proceeds with conventional recovery with the congestion window set to no more than 3 * MSS.
sections.eli5: With a more detailed receipt, the sender can see exactly which packets arrived, so it can spot a false alarm even when the replies come back out of order.

sections.title: After Detection and Use with SCTP
sections.content:
F-RTO only detects spurious timeouts. It does not say how to respond. The RFC points to RFC 4015 for a response algorithm and notes that responses differ in whether the timeout counts as a congestion signal or the congestion state is fully reverted. In general, the sender should stop retransmitting based on the timeout, and a sender in congestion avoidance should keep sending previously unsent segments.

The algorithm also applies to the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (RFC 2960), whose T3-rtx timer works like the TCP retransmission timer. Because SCTP uses selective acknowledgments, the SACK-based variant is recommended. For multi-homed associations where retransmissions go to alternative addresses, the RFC recommends conservative congestion control actions. Forward transmissions in step 2 should go to the primary address. Acknowledgments of data chunks bundled into the RTO retransmission must not be used to declare the timeout spurious.
sections.eli5: Finding the false alarm is one job, and deciding what to do next is another. This memo does the first job. It also works for a sister protocol called SCTP that has similar timers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main threat is a receiver misleading the sender into setting too large a congestion window after an RTO. The RFC considers two ways: acknowledging data it has not received, or delaying the acknowledgment of a segment it has received and acknowledging it after the sender has entered step 3.

The first is unlikely to help the receiver, because the sender cannot retransmit a segment that never reached the receiver. For the second, the RFC suggests that when an RTO expires during fast recovery, the sender should not fully revert the congestion window even if the timeout was declared spurious, and should reduce the congestion window to 1 instead. If more than one segment is missing at the time of the timeout, misleading the sender gains the receiver nothing, because another recovery period is needed anyway.
sections.eli5: A sneaky receiver could lie to make the sender go faster. The memo explains why the lie usually does not pay off and suggests a cautious rule for the risky case.
